short_description: Short Gram-positive, non-sporing rod, only about 0.4-0.5 x 1-2 um, that hides inside the host-cell cytoplasm after breaking out of its phagosome, and there hijacks the host's own actin machinery: the surface protein ActA, clustered at one pole, fires up the host Arp2/3 complex to build a dense unipolar 'comet tail' of polymerised host actin that rockets the bacterium through the cytoplasm and rams it into the neighbouring cell.

labels.en: ActA surface protein at the old pole
Individual host actin filaments in the tail
VASP / profilin at the growing tail tip

do_not_draw: Any endospore, forespore or sporangium swelling in the cell — Listeria does NOT sporulate; this is the single most common confusion with Clostridium/Bacillus and is a hard fail for this species.

A Gram-negative double envelope: no outer membrane, no membrane-periplasm-membrane sandwich, no LPS / O-antigen fringe. Listeria is Gram-positive (plasma membrane plus one thick peptidoglycan wall only).
A capsule — Listeria monocytogenes does not produce one.
A coccus, sphere, diplococcus or bead-chain shape — it is a short rod/coccobacillus.
A long slender filament many times longer than wide, like C. difficile or Bacillus — Listeria is SHORT, roughly only 2-4x longer than wide, near-coccobacillary.

The actin comet tail drawn as a flagellum, a single smooth solid rudder or blade, a fish tail, a rocket exhaust flame, or with motion lines / speed streaks / a starburst radiating from the cell. It must read as a bushy, irregular meshwork of many short branching actin filaments, not a single continuous shape.
The actin tail at both poles, at the sides, or wrapped all around the cell — it is strictly unipolar, streaming from one old pole only.

A dense polar tuft of many flagella — real flagella here are few (roughly 1-5) and peritrichous (scattered over the body), never a polar tuft, and should be shown as sparse/optional since they are repressed at 37 C.
A mesosome (chemical-fixation artefact, not a real structure).
Membrane-bound organelles inside the bacterium — no nucleus, mitochondria, ER or Golgi in the bacterial cell.
Free-floating placement in open water or air with a blue sky background — the correct context is inside a host cell's cytoplasm, ideally with a hint of host membrane or the ruptured phagosome nearby.
Saturated 'true colour' implying a real pigment — this species is colourless/unpigmented; all colour here is a didactic legend.
colour_note: Listeria monocytogenes has no pigment. Colonies on plate are small, translucent, and appear blue-grey under Henry oblique transmitted light (the diagnostic 'ground-glass' sheen used in classical identification); on blood agar it shows only a narrow zone of beta-haemolysis, which is lysis of the red-cell medium by listeriolysin O, not a visible cell colour. Every colour in a published SEM/TEM of this organism is therefore false colour, and colour in these renders is purely a didactic legend, held identical across all four styles: sage-green peptidoglycan cell wall, violet plasma membrane, warm ivory-amber bacterial cytoplasm, dusty blue-purple nucleoid, teal ribosomes, coral-pink flagella, and gold/ochre for the ActA protein clustered at the tail-forming pole. The actin comet tail itself is rendered in a COOL PALE BLUE-WHITE, deliberately a different colour family from every bacterial structure, so the viewer immediately reads it as host material being hijacked, not part of the bacterium; the surrounding host-cell cytoplasm is a muted dusky mauve to keep the intracellular context legible without competing with the tail.

morphology_notes: Listeria monocytogenes is a short, Gram-positive, non-branching, non-sporing rod to coccobacillus, roughly 0.4-0.5 um in diameter and 1-2 um long (CDC/ASM teaching figures), i.e. for illustration only about two to four times longer than wide, distinctly stubbier than the long slender rods of Clostridioides or Bacillus. Envelope inside-out: plasma membrane, then a single thick Gram-positive peptidoglycan wall carrying wall teichoic acids; there is NO outer membrane and NO LPS, and no capsule is produced by this species. Motility is temperature-gated rather than constitutive: cells express a small number (roughly one to six) of peritrichous flagella and are actively motile with a characteristic tumbling motion when grown at or below about 30 C, but flagellar gene transcription is shut down at mammalian body temperature (37 C) so that most cells in the host are non-motile and immunologically 'quiet' with respect to flagellin/TLR5 recognition. The molecular switch is well characterised: the transcriptional repressor MogR silences the flagellar regulon at 37 C, while at or below 30 C the antirepressor GmaR (itself a thermosensor that is a folded, MogR-neutralising monomer in the cold but aggregates and loses that activity as temperature rises) binds and blocks MogR, permitting flagellar synthesis (PMC9638930). The intracellular life cycle is the organism's defining feature and the centrepiece of this illustration. Entry into normally non-phagocytic host cells is driven by two surface invasins, internalin A (InlA), which binds the host adherens-junction protein E-cadherin, and internalin B (InlB), which binds the receptor tyrosine kinase Met/HGF-receptor; both trigger receptor-mediated endocytosis-like uptake into a membrane-bound vacuole (phagosome). The bacterium then ruptures this vacuole within minutes using the pore-forming, cholesterol-dependent cytolysin listeriolysin O (LLO, hly gene product, active mainly at the acidic vacuolar pH so that it does not simply lyse the plasma membrane), assisted by two secreted phospholipases, PlcA (phosphatidylinositol-specific) and PlcB (broad-specificity, also called lecithinase), encoded in the same LIPI-1 pathogenicity island; InlB has also been shown to help drive Rab7 recruitment and early phagosomal escape independently of LLO (PMC9973280). Once free in the host cytosol, the bacterium expresses ActA, a surface protein whose distribution is deliberately asymmetric, concentrated at the pole of the bacterium that grew earliest (the 'old' pole from the previous division), so that essentially all actin nucleation happens at one end of the cell. ActA mimics the activity of host WASP/N-WASP nucleation-promoting factors, directly recruiting and activating the host Arp2/3 complex to nucleate a dense, branched network of new actin filaments at the bacterial surface, while host VASP and profilin accelerate filament elongation at the growing (bacterium-proximal) end of the tail. Continuous actin polymerisation at the ActA pole, with the resulting filament network 'ratcheting' backward as new monomers are added at the bacterial surface, propels the cell forward through the cytoplasm; reported speeds range roughly from about 0.02 up to 1.4 um/s depending on cell type and ActA polarity, and motion can be smoothly processive or saltatory (brief pauses of 10-20 s while a new tail nucleates) rather than perfectly constant. The tail itself, sometimes called a 'comet tail', is host material, not a bacterial appendage: a comet-shaped brush of many short, cross-linked, branching actin filaments (an Arp2/3-branched dendritic network, distinct from a single cable), extending typically several micrometres behind the bacterium, that stays behind as the bacterium moves and slowly depolymerises. When a motile bacterium reaches the host plasma membrane it pushes outward into a finger-like double-membrane protrusion that is engulfed by a neighbouring cell, allowing direct cell-to-cell spread without ever re-entering the extracellular space, after which the process (vacuole rupture, ActA-driven motility) repeats in the new host cell. Physiologically, L. monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular, facultative anaerobic, catalase-positive, oxidase-negative organism; it is notably psychrotrophic, able to grow slowly down to about 0-4 C (standard refrigeration, generation times on the order of 30-40 hours at 4 C) and is unusually salt- and acid-tolerant (growth reported up to roughly 10% NaCl), which is why it can persist and slowly multiply in refrigerated ready-to-eat foods that receive no further cooking. On blood agar it produces a narrow zone of beta-haemolysis attributable to LLO and gives a positive CAMP-type reaction. Clinically this adds up to listeriosis: usually mild febrile gastroenteritis in healthy adults, but invasive disease (bacteraemia, meningitis/meningoencephalitis) with substantial mortality in neonates, the elderly, and the immunocompromised, and a particular tropism for placental tissue in pregnancy (InlA/InlB-mediated crossing of the placental barrier) that can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm delivery or neonatal sepsis. Recognised food vehicles are unpasteurised/raw-milk soft cheeses, smoked or cured fish, deli meats and cold cuts, hot dogs, and pre-packaged salads; because the organism survives and grows cold, guidance for high-risk groups (heating deli meats to steaming, avoiding unpasteurised soft cheese) rather than refrigeration alone is emphasised, and thorough cooking (>70 C core) reliably kills it. Sources are broadly consistent on all points above; the main variability in the literature is quantitative (exact cell dimensions, exact motility speed range, exact number of flagella) rather than a disagreement about mechanism, and is flagged with 'roughly' throughout above.
